newsitem.title: CHINA: China stock offer heats up car sector, raises fears.
newsitem.headline: China stock offer heats up car sector, raises fears.

text.p: A big Chinese automaker's plans to offer 2 billion yuan worth of stock is likely to heat up competition in the sluggish domestic car sector, analysts said on Thursday.
The move is also raising eyebrows as it highlights the pitfalls of foreign companies transferring technology to China, they said.

First Auto Works, based in the northeast city of Changchun, said this week it would issue 300 million A shares for domestic investors and list them on the southern stock exchange of Shenzhen next month.
First Auto has a number of joint ventures, including one with big German automaker Volkswagen AG making Jetta cars and another with Volkswagen's Audi arm building a version of the Audi 200.

The share offer appears to give First Auto, a big state-run producer of trucks, a badly needed cash injection that would allow it to try to take on its joint venture partners in the passenger car marketplace.
"This at least shows the pitfalls of some technology transfer arrangements," said an analyst who asked not to be named.
First Auto would use the funds to expand the now modest production of its Hongqi (Red Flag) passenger car to reach 90,000 cars a year by 2001.
First Auto had a separate licensing agreement with Audi that gave it access to technology from the German carmaker. The accord expired in 1996.
Volkswagen has said the Hongqi was based on an Audi model.
"It is actually an Audi car with another engine and a little modification of the front end," said a Volkswagen official in Beijing.
First Auto disputes this.
"The Red Flag we are producing is entirely a domestically made vehicle," said a First Auto official, speaking by telephone from Changchun.
"We have absorbed some Audi and Volkswagen technology but it is China's own product."
The Chinese automaker also maintains it is aiming at a different segment of the market than the more expensive Audi.
China has been lobbying hard for technology transfer in key industries. An auto industry policy announced in 1994 requires technology transfer for foreign participation in the domestic industry.
The prospect of sharply expanded production is likely to unsettle some manufacturers in the domestic industry, many of them already struggling to make a profit.
"Installed capacity does appear to be running ahead of demand," said an analyst.
"Profit margins in this industry are likely to be small for some time though they could get big later."
Tight controls on bank credit coupled with regional protectionism and competition from imports have hampered sales of locally built cars and pushed up stockpiles.

Chinese officials have said French carmaker Peugeot is in the final stages of pulling out of its joint venture in the southern city of Guangzhou, though several other car makers are said to be in talks to take its place.
U.S. auto giant General Motors is also moving ahead with a $1.5 billion joint venture project.
China produced about 1.6 million motor vehicles last year, including about 400,000 cars. Forecasts have put total production at 2.7 million vehicles by the year 2000.
